unit.title: Perform wet hair styling and roller placement

summary: This unit teaches you to shape hair while it is wet: consult with the client, prepare the hair, choose setting products, roller sizes and base placements, section and wind rollers correctly, make pin curls and finger waves, and set natural hair with flexi-rods and perm rods. You will also learn to dry the set safely under a hood dryer, remove the rollers, dress out a finished style, give aftercare advice and clean your tools.

blocks.p: A wet set is one of the oldest and most useful skills in the salon. Hair is shaped while it is damp, held in that shape with rollers, pins or clips while it dries, and then dressed out into the finished style. It gives smooth waves, curls, volume and body, it can be done on relaxed, natural and stretched hair, and it is the base for many Jamaican salon styles, from a classic roller set for church to a flexi-rod set on natural hair. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

A good set looks easy and is not. It depends on a clean parting, an even section, the right roller, the right base, smooth ends, even tension and a set that is **completely dry** before it is taken down. Each of these is a skill you will practise until it is automatic.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the first, you give a full-head roller set to a training head or model, planned on a sketch, with large rollers on base on top, half-off base on the crown and sides and off base at the nape, in a brick pattern, then dry, cool and dress it out. In the second, you make finger-wave ridges and flat pin curls, and give a flexi-rod set to textured hair.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Photograph only the hair and the work area. Never photograph a model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Hair is made of the protein keratin. The keratin chains are held in their shape by **bonds**. The ones that matter for a wet set are the **hydrogen bonds**. They are weak and temporary, and **water breaks them**. When hair is wet, it can be stretched and moulded. If you hold it in the new shape while it dries, the hydrogen bonds **re-form** in the new position, and the hair keeps the shape until it gets wet again. That is why a roller set holds.

head: Stage
What happens to the hair
rows: Dry hair
Hydrogen bonds hold the hair in its natural shape (straight, wavy or curly).
Wet hair
Water breaks the hydrogen bonds. The hair is soft and stretches easily, so it can be moulded.
Held in a new shape while drying
As the water leaves, the bonds re-form **in the new shape**.
Dry set
The hair holds the curl or wave until the next time it gets wet.

blocks.note: A wet set is a **temporary** change. It does not use chemicals and does not change the hair's structure, so it lasts only until the hair is wet again, or until the hair takes in moisture from the air.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Hair takes in moisture from humid air, and the hydrogen bonds loosen again. In humid weather and on rainy days, a set drops, goes frizzy or loses its curl much sooner. Jamaica is humid for much of the year, so the stylist must plan for it and the client must know how to protect the set.

ul: Use a **firmer setting product** and a slightly **smaller roller** than usual, since the curl will relax.
**Dry the set completely**: any damp hair left inside the roller drops quickly.
Finish with a light, humidity-resistant hairspray.
Advise the client to wrap or cover the hair at night and to keep an umbrella or shower cap with her.

blocks.h: Wet setting on different hair types

head: Hair
How it is set
Notes
rows: Relaxed hair
Rollers (smooth plastic, pinned), pin curls, finger waves, wrap set
Smooth, full result. Handle the line of demarcation gently.
Natural or textured hair
Flexi-rods, perm rods, twist-and-curl and roller sets on stretched hair
Detangle fully and gently, keep the hair damp, allow for **shrinkage**: coily hair draws up as it dries.
Chemically treated or fragile hair
Larger rollers, lower tension and heat
Hair that is porous or weak breaks more easily under tension.

ul: Ask what style she wants, where she is going and for **how long the set must last**: a wedding or a funeral on one day, a week at work, the weekend.
Ask about her hair: relaxed or natural, any colour, heat styling, recent treatments, and what she uses at home.
Look at the hair and scalp in good light: length, density, texture, condition, regrowth and scalp problems. A scalp condition that stops other services may stop this one too.
Ask about health or comfort: a sore neck, dizziness or high blood pressure that might make time under the hood dryer a problem.
Look at any photo with her, and say honestly what her hair can do.
Agree the style, the time and the price, and write the plan on her record card.

blocks.p: Before you wind a single roller, decide on the plan. Many stylists sketch the head and mark the roller sizes and base positions. The plan answers four questions: **Where** does she want volume? **How much** curl or wave? **Which direction** will the style go? **What size** rollers will give it?

blocks.h: Preparing the hair and the client

flow: Blot with a towel to damp

ul: Gown the client with a towel and waterproof cape for the shampoo, then a dry towel or collar for the set.
**Shampoo** with a gentle shampoo. Use a **light conditioner** or none: heavy conditioners weigh the hair down and make the set drop.
**Detangle** completely, starting at the ends and working up to the roots with a wide-tooth comb. Never wind tangled hair.
**Blot** the hair with a towel so that it is **evenly damp**, not dripping and not nearly dry. Hair that is too wet takes too long to dry and sets weakly; hair that has dried partly sets poorly.
If any part dries out while you are working, **re-dampen it with a water spray** before you wind it.

blocks.note: Wash your hands before you start. Keep water and electrical tools apart, and keep the floor dry. Jamaica's supply is 110 V at 50 Hz; dry your hands before you touch a plug.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Tool
What it is for
rows: Tail comb
Parting and taking clean, straight sections; smoothing hair over a roller.
Wide-tooth comb
Detangling from the ends; combing setting lotion through.
Sectioning clips
Holding hair out of the way while you work.
Rollers
Smooth plastic, mesh, brush, magnetic or foam rollers in different diameters: the roller size decides the curl.
Roller pins (picks)
Hold a roller in place. Pushed through the roller to its base, **without touching the scalp**.
Flexi-rods
Bendy foam rods: wind along the strand for spiral curls on natural hair.
Perm rods
Small plastic rods with a band; used with no perm solution for defined small curls.
Sponge rollers
Soft rollers a client can sleep in comfortably at home.
End papers
Thin tissue folded over the ends so they lie smooth on the roller and do not bend or frizz.
Double-prong clips
Hold pin curls and waves in place.
Hair net
Holds rollers in place while the hair dries.
Ear protectors
Protect the ears from the heat of the hood dryer.
Spray bottle
Re-dampens the hair.
Hood dryer
Dries the set with warm air.
Bristle or cushion brush
Brushes the dry set out, to blend the curls.

head: Roller size
What it gives
Used for
rows: Small
The tightest curl
Short hair; tight curl; the nape and short ends
Medium
A medium curl or wave
Most of the head on shoulder-length hair
Large
Soft, loose waves and the **most volume** and lift
The top and crown; long hair; a smooth, full finish

ul: A roller's size is the width it winds the hair around. The **smaller** the roller, the **tighter** the curl; the **larger**, the softer the wave.
The length of the hair matters: long hair needs a bigger roller to wind the length without too many turns, and short hair needs a smaller one, or the hair will not make a full turn.
For **relaxed** hair and a smooth, full finish, use **smooth plastic rollers** held with pins.
Choose smaller rollers than the curl you want if the weather is humid, since the curl will relax.

head: Product
What it does
How to use it
rows: Setting lotion
Helps the set hold its shape and last longer; adds body and sometimes shine.
Apply evenly through towel-dried hair from roots to ends, then comb through. The firmer the lotion, the firmer the hold.
Setting foam or mousse
Light hold and body; suits finer or natural hair.
Work through damp hair in sections.
Curl cream or setting foam for natural hair
Moisture, definition and hold for coily hair.
Apply to each small, damp section before winding a flexi-rod.
Styling gel
A strong hold; used for finger waves.
Apply to wet hair, and comb smooth. Too much leaves the hair stiff, flaky and slow to dry.
Leave-in conditioner
Light moisture; helps detangling.
On natural hair before the curl cream.

blocks.note: Do not use too much of any setting product. It makes the hair stiff, sticky and slow to dry, leaves white flakes when it is brushed out, and gives a heavy look. Follow the maker's instructions.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Sectioning, base control and winding rollers

blocks.p: The **base** is the section of scalp that a roller sits on. Its size and the angle at which you hold the hair away from the head decide how much **volume** (lift at the roots) the set will have.

head: Placement
How the hair is held while you wind
Where the roller sits
Result
Used for
rows: **On base**
Up and slightly forward, over the base, at about 135 degrees
Directly **on** its base
The **most volume** at the roots
The top, from the front hairline to the crown
**Half-off base**
Straight out from the head, at **90 degrees**
Half on the base, half off it
Medium volume and lift
The crown and upper sides; blending between the top and the lower areas
**Off base**
Down, below 90 degrees (about 45 degrees)
Completely **off** its base, below it
Little or no volume; curl at the ends
The nape and lower sides; smooth ends curling under

ul: The **base section** should be about **as long and as wide as the roller**. A section that is too big means the hair is stretched and bunched; too small leaves a loose, empty roller.
Each section is taken with the **tail comb**, with a clean, straight parting, and combed smooth from roots to ends.
Sections must be **clean and even**, so that each roller holds the same amount of hair and the set is even.

blocks.p: Rollers are placed in a **brick pattern**, like bricks in a wall: each row is offset from the one above it, so that the base sections do not line up. This leaves **no gaps or straight parting lines** in the set when it is brushed out. At the back, a brick pattern is used with the rows following the shape of the head.

blocks.h: Winding one roller, step by step

flow: Hair damp and combed; lotion on
Take a clean section about the size of the roller
Hold it at the angle for the base
End paper over short or fine ends
Place the roller under the ends, ends smooth and flat
Wind down to the scalp with even tension
Secure with a pin through the roller to its base

ul: Hold the hair at the correct angle for the base: up and over for on base, straight out for half-off base, down for off base.
Place the roller under the ends, which must lie **smooth and spread across the roller**, with no bends. Use **end papers** on short or fine ends to hold them flat.
Wind the roller down towards the scalp with **even, firm tension**. Even tension gives a smooth, even curl from root to end.
A roller that is **too tight** stretches the hair, can break it and can make the scalp sore. A roller that is **too loose** slips out and leaves a weak curl.
Fasten with a **roller pin** through the roller and into the base, **without touching the scalp**. A pin that presses on the scalp is painful, and over a long drying time it can burn.
Check that the client is comfortable before moving on.

blocks.p: **Directional winding** means placing the rollers to follow the direction the hair will be worn. For a style that sweeps back from the face, wind the front rollers back; for a style with a side parting, wind them towards the side. The direction you wind sets the direction the hair will fall.

head: Method
How it is done
Result
rows: Croquignole
The hair is wound **from the ends towards the roots**, so that each turn lies on top of the last.
Curls that are tight and short at the ends and bigger at the roots; the usual roller method.
Spiral
The hair is wound **along the strand**, in a coil, like a spring.
Long ringlets; used with flexi-rods and spiral rods.

head: Fault
Cause
Cure
rows: Fish hook (a bent or crooked end)
Ends folded or bent on the roller; no end paper on short ends
Smooth the ends flat before you wind; use end papers
Gaps and split lines in the set
Sections not even; rollers not in a brick pattern
Section cleanly and offset each row
Uneven curl
Uneven sections or tension
Take sections the size of the roller; wind with even tension
Flat, no volume at the roots
Hair held down; roller off base
Hold the hair up and wind on base
Breakage, sore scalp
Rollers wound too tightly
Wind with firm but not tight tension; check the client
Frizz after drying
Hair not damp enough when wound; partly dried hair
Re-dampen before winding

blocks.p: A pin curl is a coil of damp hair, flattened and clipped to dry in a circle. Pin curls give soft curls, waves and fine ends, and are used for short hair, for the ends of finger waves and for sets where rollers would be too big.

head: Part of a pin curl
What it is
What it does
rows: **Base**
The section of scalp the curl sits on (the shape of the section: a square, a triangle or a half-moon)
Holds the curl
**Stem**
The hair between the base and the circle
Gives the curl its **direction and movement**
**Circle**
The curled part of the hair
Decides the size of the curl: a bigger circle gives a softer curl

head: Stem length
Where the circle sits
Result
rows: No stem
Right on the base
A firm, tight, long-lasting curl; the least movement
Half stem
Half off the base
More movement; a medium curl
Full stem
Off the base, well along the stem
The most movement; the loosest result

head: Type of curl
Description
Result
rows: Flat pin curl
Lies flat against the head
Waves and flat curls; used in finger waves
Barrel (stand-up) curl
Stands up from the head on its base
Volume and lift
Open-centre curl
The circle is the **same size from the centre to the outside**
An **even** curl and a smooth wave
Closed-centre curl
The circle gets smaller towards the centre
A curl that is tight in the middle and wide at the end; a more uneven wave

flow: Part a section: a square or triangle
Comb smooth, in the direction of the curl
Wind the ends round your finger to make a circle
Lay it flat on its base
Clip through the circle at the base, not across the stem

ul: Keep the **ends inside** the circle, so that they do not stick out and kink.
Clip with a **double-prong clip** through the circle **at the base**, **without crossing the stem**. A clip that crosses the stem leaves a dent in the hair.
Make every curl in a row go the **same way**, with the same size circle, so that the wave is even.
Do not push the clip into the scalp. Ask the client if it is comfortable.

blocks.p: **Finger waves** are S-shaped waves formed on wet hair with the fingers and a comb. They suit hair that is at least a few centimetres long and are often finished with pin curls at the ends.

flow: Wet hair with gel or lotion
Comb in the direction of the first wave
Index finger above the first ridge
Comb the hair under your finger
Press hair between finger and comb: ridge
Comb the next section the opposite way
Form the second ridge: an S shape

ul: Apply a setting lotion or gel generously to **wet** hair and comb it smooth, so that the hair is slippery and easy to mould.
The raised line between two waves is called the **ridge**. The hollow between ridges is the trough.
Place your index finger just above where the first ridge will be, and comb the hair forward under it about 2 to 3 cm, then press the hair together between your finger and the comb to form the ridge.
Form the next ridge by combing in the **opposite direction**, making the S shape.
Keep the waves an **even width** and follow the shape of the head.
Finish the ends with a row of pin curls, put on a net and ear protectors, and dry under the hood dryer. Let the waves **cool** before taking down the net and the clips.

sections.title: Wet sets on natural hair, and the wrap set

blocks.h: Flexi-rod and perm-rod sets on natural hair

blocks.p: A flexi-rod or perm-rod set gives natural hair soft, defined curls without heat or chemicals. The curl keeps the hair's texture. It dries into a neat set and gives a 'stretched' look to start a style. The set needs patience: coily hair has to be fully detangled, kept damp and dried completely.

flow: Shampoo in sections; moisturising shampoo; condition
Detangle each section from the ends up
Keep damp with a spray bottle
Leave-in conditioner, then curl cream or foam
Take small sections the width of the rod
Wind along the strand to the scalp, even tension
Dry fully under a hood dryer, medium heat

ul: **Detangle fully** before you start. Winding tangled coily hair makes the curl rough and can snap the hair.
Use **small sections**, about as wide as the rod. Large sections give loose, uneven curls that dry slowly.

On a **flexi-rod**, place the end of the hair on the rod and wind it **along the strand** towards the scalp, smoothly and evenly, then bend the ends of the rod to hold it. On a **perm rod**, wind from the ends to the roots and fasten the band without pressing on the hair.
Use a **curl cream or setting foam** and a leave-in conditioner. Do not use a heavy gel that makes the hair stiff.

Drying takes a long time: natural hair is thick and holds water. Use a medium heat, check the client often, and make sure the hair is **completely dry** before taking the rods out. Damp coils will frizz and lose definition.
Remove the rods gently and **separate the curls** with oiled or moisturised fingers. Do not brush.
Allow for **shrinkage**. Coily hair draws up as it dries and can look much shorter. Tell the client what to expect.

blocks.h: The wrap set on relaxed hair

blocks.p: A **wrap set** (or wrap) gives relaxed hair a smooth, swinging style. Wet hair is combed smoothly round the head in one direction and dried flat; it is then combed out into a straight style that swings.

flow: Comb smooth round the head, in one direction
Keep the hair flat and close to the scalp
Place a roller at the crown if height is wanted

ul: Work from the parting, combing each section **smoothly over the next** so that the whole head is wrapped in a circle, following the shape of the head.
Keep the hair **close to the scalp** with no gaps or ridges.
Dry completely under the hood dryer and let it cool before combing out.
Advise the client to wrap the hair again at night with a satin scarf, and to keep it away from water and humid air.

sections.title: Drying, removing rollers and dressing out

blocks.h: Drying the set under a hood dryer

flow: Check the dryer: plug, cable, hood
Adjust the hood; set the heat
Test dryness at the crown and nape

ul: Check the dryer before the client sits down: the **plug, cable and hood** must be undamaged, and it must work. Do not use a faulty dryer; report it.
Put a **hair net** over the rollers, to hold them in place, and place **ear protectors** (or cotton wool) over the ears. **The ears can get too hot and burn** under the hood.
Seat the client comfortably with her back supported. Adjust the hood so that it covers the rollers **without pressing on them**, and keep the hood off her ears and face.

Set the heat and time to suit her hair: usually **medium** heat. Fine, damaged or chemically treated hair needs a lower heat. A set often takes 30 to 45 minutes or more, and natural hair under a flexi-rod set takes longer. Follow the dryer maker's instructions and your instructor.
Ask how the heat feels, and **check on her every 10 minutes or so**. If she says it is too hot, **turn it down at once** and check her scalp and ears.
Give her something to read and water to drink, and make sure her belongings are safe.
Do not leave a client under a dryer alone for long. Never leave her asleep with the dryer on at high heat.

blocks.h: Checking that the set is dry

blocks.p: Unwind **one roller at the crown and one at the nape**, the thickest and slowest-drying areas, and feel the hair. It must be completely dry, not cool and damp. If it feels cool or damp, put the roller back and dry longer. Hair that is taken down damp drops quickly, goes frizzy and loses its curl.

ul: Switch off, lift the hood, and let the set **cool** before you take it down. Hair holds its new shape as it cools; curls taken out while hot are soft and drop sooner.
Take out the pins first, then remove the rollers **gently, starting at the nape and working up** to the top. Unwind each one without pulling, so that the curl is not stretched.
Put the rollers and pins straight into a bowl to be cleaned.

blocks.p: **Dressing out** is brushing out and shaping the curls into the finished style.

flow: Let the curls sit a moment
Brush through gently with a bristle or cushion brush
Shape with hands and brush into the agreed style
Back-comb lightly at the roots for height, if wanted
Light hairspray or shine spray; shield the face
Show her the back with a hand mirror

ul: Brush **gently**. Heavy brushing breaks up the curl and pulls on hair that is weakest where it has been wound.
Back-combing, if used, is light and at the roots, and is always brushed out gently at the end of the day.
Check the balance of the style from the front and both sides.
Protect the client's face and eyes when you use spray.
Wrap the hair or wear a **satin bonnet or scarf** at night; sleep on satin.
Keep the set away from water, steam and humid air: use a shower cap and an umbrella.
Do not touch the curls too much or brush them heavily.
Keep the scalp and hair moisturised.
Do not wash the hair until the set has gone; return for the next set as advised.

head: Hazard
Risk
What you do
rows: Hood dryer heat
Burns to the scalp and ears; overheating
Ear protectors; medium heat; check often; turn down at once if she says it is too hot
Electrical equipment near water
Shock, fire
Keep dryers and cables away from basins and wet floors; dry hands; check plugs and cables; report damage
Rollers pinned into the scalp, or wound too tightly
Pain, a sore scalp, broken hair
Pins through the roller, not on the scalp; even, firm tension
Wet floors
Slips
Wipe up spills; wet floor sign
Hair and tools left on the floor
Slips, cross-infection
Sweep; clean and disinfect any tool that is dropped
Bent pins, cracked rollers
They catch and tear the hair
Throw them away
A long time at the chair
Back and shoulder strain for you; discomfort for the client
Adjust the chair height; stand straight; give the client a break if needed

flow: Store in a clean, covered container

ul: After every client, remove **all the hair** from combs, rollers, rods, pins and clips.

**Wash** in warm, soapy water, rinse, then **disinfect** in a solution mixed as the label says for the **full contact time**. Cleaning always comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt and hair.
Store the tools in a clean, **covered** container.
Wash hair nets, or throw away single-use ones. Throw away used end papers.
Wipe the hood dryer with a suitable disinfectant when it is **cool and unplugged**, and report any fault.
Fresh towels, gown and cape for every client; used ones go straight into a closed laundry bin.

blocks.p: Write the date, the style, the roller sizes and base placements, the setting product and the drying time, the condition of the hair and scalp, any problems and the aftercare given. The next stylist can then repeat or change a style that worked.

ul: I can explain why a wet set holds, with the hydrogen bonds and water.
I can explain why a set drops or goes frizzy in humid weather and what to do about it.
I can carry out a consultation for a set and plan the roller sizes and bases on a sketch.
I can prepare the hair: shampoo, light conditioner, detangle and blot to even dampness.
I can choose the roller size for the curl and the volume the client wants.
I can name the main tools and say what each is for.
I can choose and apply a setting lotion, foam, gel or curl cream, and not too much.
I can define the base and take clean, even sections the size of the roller.
I can place rollers on base, half-off base and off base, and say what each gives.
I can place rollers in a brick pattern and wind them directionally.
I can wind a roller correctly: smooth ends, end papers, even tension, secured without touching the scalp.
I can tell spiral and croquignole winding apart.
I can avoid and correct fish hooks and other roller faults.
I can name the parts of a pin curl and make and clip a flat pin curl.
I can form finger-wave ridges and S-shaped waves.
I can give a flexi-rod or perm-rod set on detangled natural hair and allow for shrinkage.
I can give a wrap set on relaxed hair.
I can dry a set safely under a hood dryer and check that it is completely dry.
I can let the set cool, remove the rollers from the nape up, and dress out the style.
I can give aftercare advice, clean and disinfect rollers and tools, and record the service.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each choice: for example, 'I use large rollers on base on top, because the large size gives soft waves and the on-base position gives the most lift.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Wet set
Shaping damp hair on rollers, pins or rods and drying it so that it keeps the new shape.
Hydrogen bonds
Weak, temporary bonds in the hair that water breaks and that re-form in the new shape as the hair dries.
Keratin
The protein that hair is made of.
Humidity
Moisture in the air, which loosens a set.
Setting lotion
A product that helps a set hold its shape.
Curl cream
A moisturising product for defining curls on natural hair.
Roller
A cylinder around which hair is wound to curl it.
Roller pin (pick)
A pin pushed through a roller to hold it in place.
Flexi-rod
A bendy foam rod used to make spiral curls.
Perm rod
A small plastic rod with a band, used without perm solution for small curls.
Sponge roller
A soft roller a client can sleep in.
End paper
Thin tissue folded over the ends of hair to keep them smooth on a roller.
Tail comb
A comb with a long, thin handle used to part clean sections.
Mesh
A thin section of hair taken to wind on one roller.
Base
The section of scalp a roller or curl sits on.
On base
A roller sitting directly on its base; gives the most volume.
Half-off base
A roller sitting half on its base, with the hair held at 90 degrees; medium volume.
Off base
A roller sitting off its base, with the hair held down; little volume, curl at the ends.
Volume
The lift and body a set has at the roots.
Brick pattern
Rollers placed offset, like bricks, so that no gaps or parting lines show.
Directional winding
Placing rollers to follow the way the hair will be worn.
Croquignole
Winding hair from the ends towards the roots.
Spiral winding
Winding hair in a coil along the strand.
Fish hook
A bent or crooked end on a curl, caused by poor winding.
Pin curl
A coil of damp hair, flattened and clipped to dry.
Stem
The hair between the base and the circle of a pin curl; gives direction and movement.
Circle
The curled part of a pin curl.
Barrel curl
A pin curl that stands up from the scalp on its base to give volume.
Open-centre curl
A curl whose circle is the same size from the centre out, giving an even wave.
Finger waves
S-shaped waves made on wet hair with fingers and a comb.
Ridge
The raised line between two finger waves.
Wrap set
Wet relaxed hair combed smoothly round the head and dried flat.
Shrinkage
Coily hair drawing up and looking shorter as it dries.
Hair net
A net that holds rollers in place while drying.
Ear protectors
Covers placed over the ears to protect them from the heat of the hood dryer.
Hood dryer
A seated dryer with a hood, used to dry a set.
Dressing out
Brushing out and shaping the curls into the finished style.
Crown
The highest part of the head, at the top towards the back.
Whorl
A spiral pattern in which the hair grows out from one point, often at the crown.
Nape
The back of the neck, where the hairline ends.
Contact time
How long a tool must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.

c1.title: A wedding set in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: Mrs. Beverley Hall, 55, has relaxed, shoulder-length hair and is the mother of the bride at an outdoor wedding in Savanna-la-Mar in July. She wants lots of lift on top and soft curls at the nape. Trainee Chevaughn shampoos her, then notices the hair is quite fine and the day will be hot and humid. He has large, medium and small smooth plastic rollers, pins, end papers and a firm-hold setting lotion.

c2.title: A set that goes wrong in Black River
c2.text: Trainee Shelly-Ann sets Miss Dahlia Facey's hair with rollers. Some rollers have a bent end sticking out, and some sit crooked against the next row so that the parting lines show. She finds that the hair at the nape has dried while she was working on the top. After a short time under the hood dryer, Miss Facey says her ears feel very hot.

c3.title: Pin curls and finger waves in Falmouth
c3.text: In the Centre's salon, trainees Rohan and Camille practise on a training head with relaxed hair. Rohan forms finger waves but his ridges are uneven in width and flatten out. Camille makes flat pin curls with a double-prong clip pushed across the stem, and when she takes the curls down, there are dents across them.

c4.title: A flexi-rod set in Montego Bay
c4.text: Miss Chantelle Powell, 29, has natural, shoulder-length, tightly coiled hair that she wears in a puff. She wants a stretched, defined curl set for a photo shoot on Saturday. Trainee Joel washes her hair, then starts winding flexi-rods onto large, thick sections. The hair is still partly tangled at the nape, and he plans to dry the set under the hood dryer for 15 minutes.

c5.title: Taking down the set in Spanish Town
c5.text: Mrs. Coleen Ricketts has been under the hood dryer for 40 minutes. Trainee Latoya, who is in a hurry for her next client, switches off the dryer and takes out the rollers from the top of the head, straight away. The hair at the crown feels cool and slightly damp. After the rollers are out she brushes the curls hard with a stiff brush.

questions.q: Which roller placement should Chevaughn use for the lift Mrs. Hall wants on top?
o: Large rollers on base
Small rollers on base
Large rollers off base
Medium rollers off base
questions.why: On base gives the most volume at the roots, and large rollers give a soft, full lift. Off base gives little volume, and small rollers give tight curl rather than lift.

questions.q: Which rollers suit the soft curls at the nape?
o: Large rollers on base, with the hair held up and forward
Small or medium rollers off base, with the hair held down
Medium rollers on base, with the hair held at 90 degrees
Large rollers half-off base, with the hair held straight out
questions.why: At the nape the aim is curl at the ends and no lift, so smaller rollers are placed off base, with the hair held down. On base or half-off base would lift the nape hair away from the neck.

questions.q: The hair is fine and the day will be hot and humid. What should Chevaughn do?
o: Use a light lotion and large rollers throughout, then take the rollers out damp
Use a heavy conditioner after the shampoo to protect the hair from the heat of the day
Use extra setting lotion and brush it out heavily so that it lasts all day long
Use the firm-hold lotion and slightly smaller rollers, and dry the set fully
questions.why: Humidity relaxes curls, so a firmer hold, slightly smaller rollers and a completely dry set help the style last. A heavy conditioner weighs the hair down, and too much product makes the hair stiff and flaky.

questions.q: How should Chevaughn arrange the rollers at the back of the head?
o: In straight rows, one under the other, so that the rows are easy to count
In random positions, so that the curls blend into each other
In a brick pattern, so that there are no gaps or straight parting lines
In one wide row, so that the hair is wound in the fewest sections
questions.why: Rows that are offset like bricks leave no gaps or straight splits when the set is brushed out. Straight rows leave parting lines.

questions.q: What caused the bent ends sticking out of some of Shelly-Ann's rollers?
o: The sections were too large for the roller, so the hair crowded together
The hair was too wet when it was wound, so the ends could not hold a curl
The rollers were left in for too long, so the ends dried and curled
The ends were folded or bent when winding, with no end paper to keep them flat
questions.why: Ends that are folded or bent on the roller dry as a fish hook. They must lie smooth and flat, with an end paper on short or fine ends.

questions.q: Why do the parting lines show between the rows of rollers?
o: The rollers were too large, so the hair spread too widely to fill them
The rows are not offset, and the sections were not clean and even
The hair was wound tightly, which always leaves parting lines
The setting lotion was too strong and made the hair stiff along the lines
questions.why: Clean, even sections and a brick pattern with each row offset leave no gaps. Tight winding causes breakage, not lines, and lotion does not cause parting lines.

questions.q: What should Shelly-Ann have done about the hair at the nape that dried while she worked?
o: Wound it as it was, as slightly damp hair sets just as well
Added more setting lotion to the dry hair and wound it at once
Re-dampened it with the water spray before winding it
Left it out of the set and combed it into place afterwards
questions.why: Hair must be evenly damp for the hydrogen bonds to re-form in the new shape. Dry patches set poorly and frizz, so they are re-dampened with the spray.

questions.q: Miss Facey says her ears feel very hot under the dryer. What should Shelly-Ann do first?
o: Tell her to bear it for a few more minutes as it is nearly finished
Turn the heat down at once and check her scalp and ears
Lift the hood off and leave her to cool down for ten minutes
Put a wet towel over the rollers to cool the hair down
questions.why: The heat is turned down at once and the ears and scalp are checked, since ears can burn under a hood. Ear protectors should have been put on before the dryer was switched on.

questions.q: Why do Rohan's finger waves have uneven ridges that flatten out?
o: The ridges were not pressed firmly and the waves were not kept an even width
The hair was too wet, so waves cannot be made on wet hair
He used too little setting gel, so the hair could be moulded too easily
He combed all the sections the same way, which makes the ridges flat
questions.why: Finger waves need firm pressing of the hair between finger and comb to form each ridge, an even width, and an opposite direction for the next section. The hair must be wet, with plenty of gel.

questions.q: In which direction is each new section combed when making finger waves?
o: The same direction as the one before, so that the ridge carries on
Straight back from the face for every section, for a smooth line
The opposite direction to the one before, forming an S shape
Towards the nape in every section, so that the waves fall down
questions.why: Each ridge goes the opposite way to the last, so that the hair forms an S shape. If they all went the same way, there would be no wave.

questions.q: What mistake did Camille make with the double-prong clip?
o: She used a double-prong clip, which cannot hold a pin curl in place
She clipped the curl too loosely, so it dried in a different shape
She put the clip on the ends, where it should go under the circle
She pushed it across the stem instead of through the circle at the base
questions.why: A clip goes through the circle at the base, without crossing the stem. A clip across the stem leaves a mark.

questions.q: Why is Joel's plan to wind large, thick sections likely to cause problems?
o: Thick sections give very tight curls that cannot be taken down easily
Flexi-rods can only be used on hair that has first been stretched with heat
Thick sections make the hair too wet for the setting product to work well
Thick sections give loose, uneven curls and are slow to dry
questions.why: Sections should be about as wide as the rod. Thick sections give loose, uneven curls and are slow to dry, so the hair frizzes.

questions.q: What should Joel do about the tangles at the nape before he winds the rods?
o: Wind the rods over the tangles, as the curl hides them
Pull a fine comb through the tangles from the roots
Spray heavy gel on to hold the tangles together
Detangle fully from the ends up with a wide-tooth comb
questions.why: Hair must be completely detangled before winding, from the ends up, with a wide-tooth comb and the hair kept damp. Winding tangles gives rough curls and breakage.

questions.q: Joel plans to dry the flexi-rod set under the hood dryer for 15 minutes. What should he be prepared for?
o: That 15 minutes will be plenty, as natural hair dries faster than relaxed hair
That the dryer should be set to high so that the set dries in the time
That the rods should be taken out while damp, and the curls dried by hand later
That natural hair under rods dries slowly, and must be checked
questions.why: Thick, natural hair holds a lot of water and under rods can take much longer than 15 minutes. It is dried on medium heat and checked, and the rods are not removed until the hair is completely dry.

questions.q: Miss Powell is surprised that her set looks shorter than her puff did. What should Joel explain?
o: The rods were wound too tightly, which pulled the length out of her hair
The setting product shortened the hair, and a lighter one would not
Coily hair shrinks as it dries, so a set looks shorter than stretched hair
Her hair was cut too short at the nape when the set was taken down
questions.why: Coily hair draws up as it dries, so a defined curl looks much shorter than the stretched length. The client should be told this before the set.

questions.q: What is wrong with the way Latoya has switched off and begun to take the set down?
o: She should have left the dryer running while she took the rollers out
She should have taken the rollers out in the order they were placed
She should have taken the rollers out before she turned the dryer off
The hair is still slightly damp and has not cooled, so the set will drop
questions.why: Hair taken down damp or warm drops quickly, goes frizzy and loses its curl. The set must be completely dry, then cooled, before the rollers come out.

questions.q: Which roller should Latoya have checked to know whether the whole set was dry?
o: One at the front hairline, which dries first and is easiest to reach
Any one at the sides, since all the hair dries at the same time
One at the crown and one at the nape, which dry slowest
The last roller she wound, since it will have had the least heat
questions.why: The crown and the nape are the thickest, slowest-drying areas. If they are dry, the rest of the set is.

questions.q: In which order should the rollers be removed?
o: From the nape upwards, unwinding each roller gently
From the top downwards, so that the curls fall into place
From the front backwards, taking out the front rollers first
Any order, as long as each roller is pulled out in one move
questions.why: Rollers come out from the nape up, gently, without pulling the curl. Pulling stretches the curl and hurts the hair.

questions.q: What is wrong with the way Latoya dressed out the set with a stiff brush?
o: A stiff brush leaves the curls too soft, so back-combing is needed
She should have brushed from the roots, so that the curl pulls out
She should have used no brush and left the curls exactly as they were
Heavy brushing breaks up the curl; a gentle cushion brush is used
questions.why: Dressing out is gentle: a bristle or cushion brush blends the curls and removes roller marks, and the hair is then shaped by hand. A stiff, hard brush breaks the curls up and pulls at the hair.

questions.q: A client with a history of dizziness will be under the hood dryer for about 40 minutes. What is the best way to look after her?
o: Use a lower heat, check often, give water, and stop if she feels faint
Use the highest heat so that the time under the dryer is short
Leave her with a magazine and check only when the 40 minutes are over
Skip the ear protectors, so that she can hear you if unwell
questions.why: A client who is prone to dizziness needs gentler, cooler drying, regular checks and a drink, and the dryer is stopped if she feels faint. High heat and long gaps between checks make it worse, and ear protectors are always used.
